faq.q: How is my score calculated?
faq.a: Distance fallen is your score, shown in meters. Every obstacle you clear also counts as a pass, and a close pass — threading a gap with almost no room to spare — adds a +5 m bonus to your distance. There is no online leaderboard; your best distance is saved in this browser.

faq.q: What kinds of hazards are there?
faq.a: Twenty-six, from solo and split bars to saws, lasers, lightning, homing drones, pendulums, crushers, and portals. Each has its own timing — saws spin at fixed speeds, lasers pulse in intervals, lightning chains punish hesitation. Learning each hazard's rhythm lets you commit earlier and thread tighter gaps.

faq.q: Where should I position myself in the shaft?
faq.a: Stay centered between threats. Committing to a wall early leaves no escape when the next pattern shifts. Center positioning maximizes your available reaction directions as patterns change.

faq.q: How do I deal with patterns at high speed?
faq.a: Read two obstacles ahead rather than one — at high shaft speeds, reacting to what is immediately in front of you is too slow. Identify the next gap before you reach the current one and begin steering toward it in advance.

faq.q: What does the Screen Changer do?
faq.a: Collecting it rotates the entire shaft 90 degrees — a vertical fall becomes a horizontal one, and the next one flips it back. Your velocity resets and held keys clear during the flip so you don't slam into a wall; re-read the new layout before you steer. Dodge past a Changer and another spawns shortly after.

24.title: Entrepreneur Tycoon
24.description: Turn one lemonade stand into a 30-industry empire on a living street market — hire managers, court whale customers, and guard your reputation as the buildings pile up.
24.fullDescription:
Entrepreneur Tycoon puts you in charge of a street of businesses. Start with a **$4 lemonade stand**, click **Produce** to run your first cycle, and reinvest every dollar into more units, more shops, and staff who keep the cycle turning while you plan the next purchase.
      **Thirty industries across ten categories** — Food, Lifestyle, Agriculture, Health, Finance, Entertainment, Travel, Tech, Real Estate, and Energy — climb from a shoeshine stand and a pizza delivery to a hedge fund, a cruise line, a chip fab, and finally a **fusion reactor**. Every industry gets its own hand-drawn building on the street, and the street grows floors as your empire does.
      Customers walk the sidewalk for real. Broke shoppers, regulars, the wealthy, and top-hatted whales pick a shop, buy, and tip — minus delivery, transaction, and platform fees. Turn a customer away with empty shelves and your reputation drops, which cuts revenue and foot traffic. **Reputation runs from 1 to 10,000** and swings your income between **half and 1.5×**, so the shady upgrades that triple revenue while leaking rep every second are a real trade, not a free lunch.
      **Unit milestones** double each shop's output, sales milestones stack on top as a shop becomes a local favorite and then a global brand, and every other industry you unlock feeds a **synergy bonus** back into the rest. Come back after a break and the game settles up to **eight hours of offline earnings**.
24.controls: Mouse: click ▶ Produce on a card to run a cycle, Buy to add units, Hire to recruit a manager or employees, and the pause toggle to stop a shop. Scroll over the street to zoom in on your buildings. Touch: tap the same buttons; buildings on the street open their card.
24.tips: Hire a manager on your first two shops as early as you can — until then every cycle needs a click. Buy toward **unit milestones (25, 50, 100…)**: each one doubles that shop's revenue. Keep stock up: every customer turned away costs reputation and money. Unlock cheap industries even when they earn little — each one adds a **synergy bonus** to all the others. Treat **Shady upgrades** as a sprint: their reputation drain never stops, so buy the regen and forgiveness upgrades first.
24.lore:
They said the block was dead. Shuttered storefronts, a bus stop nobody used, and a kid selling lemonade for **four dollars a cup** because that was all the ingredients cost.
      The kid kept the change. Then hired a manager. Then bought the shoeshine stand next door, then the allotment behind it, and one morning the street woke up to scaffolding where the empty lots used to be.
      Now the whales arrive in top hats, the tabloids sniff around for a story, and the skyline at the end of the road hums with a reactor you built. It is still your street. Keep it that way.

faq.q: Why did my shop stop producing?
faq.a: Without a manager a shop runs one cycle per click. Hire a manager from the card — recruiting takes 45 seconds — and the shop restarts its cycle automatically from then on.

faq.q: What does reputation do?
faq.a: Reputation runs from 1 to 10,000 and starts at 1,000, the neutral point (×1.0 revenue). Below it your revenue slides toward 0.5×, above it climbs toward 1.5×, and the climb slows near the top. It also scales how many customers walk the street and shrinks penalties when it is high. Sold-out shops that turn customers away, firing staff, shady upgrades and unpaid payroll all cost reputation; customer upgrades add regen and forgiveness.

faq.q: Are Shady upgrades worth it?
faq.a: They give the biggest multipliers in the game — ×3 revenue, ×3 tips, +80% foot traffic — but each one drains reputation every second for the rest of the run. Buy reputation regen first, or take them late when you can afford the hit.

faq.q: How do customers make money?
faq.a: Each customer who buys pays a tip on top of the shop's cycle revenue: 5% of the unit price, multiplied by their wealth tier (whales pay 8×). Delivery, transaction, and platform fees take a cut of every tip. Customer upgrades raise foot traffic, wealthy and whale odds, and tip size.

faq.q: What are unit and sales milestones?
faq.a: Owning 25, 50, 100, 150, 200, 250 and 300 units of an industry doubles its revenue at each step. Separately, selling 50, 250, 1,000… units to street customers raises that shop through Regulars, Local favorite, City landmark, and up to Global empire at ×25. Both stack with your upgrades and synergy.

faq.q: Does the game progress while I'm away?
faq.a: Yes. Your save lives in the browser and the game catches up on up to 8 hours of production when you return. Managed shops keep cycling; unmanaged ones finish the cycle they were on.

25.title: Vault of Ashes: Fallen Era
25.description: A grim loadout-driven grid auto-battler — assemble blades, wards, and alchemy across an arcane grid, then watch your build fight on its own through the ruins of a fallen age.
25.fullDescription:
Vault of Ashes: Fallen Era is a **loadout-focused grid auto-battler** set in a kingdom devoured by an **eclipse**. You don't control the fight directly — you build it. Slot weapons, armor, potions, and runes onto a **tactical grid** before each run, then watch your hooded vanguard cut through waves of **fallen knights**, cinder-wraiths, and gate-born horrors.
      Every cell on the grid matters. **Adjacency** unlocks synergies: a **flame-blade beside an ember rune** deals burn ticks; a shield beside a vitality flask trades attack speed for survival. The wrong arrangement loses runs before the first sword swing — the right one shreds bosses in seconds.
      Loot dropped from each chapter expands your **vault**. Rotate gear between runs, hunt **set bonuses**, and chase **legendary anchor pieces** that reshape entire builds. The fallen era doesn't reward reflexes. It rewards preparation.
      The vault is sealed. The eclipse is bleeding. Will your loadout hold the line, or will you join the ash?
25.controls: Mouse Click: Place gear onto grid cells and confirm loadout / Mouse Drag: Rearrange equipped items / Mouse Click (Combat UI): Trigger ultimate abilities and view stats.
25.tips: **Adjacency** is everything — never place a rune alone if a matching weapon could sit beside it. Save **legendary anchor pieces** for builds you've already validated in early chapters; rerolling around them mid-run wastes **vault** slots. When two builds tie on damage, the one with a **dedicated potion column** survives longer boss phases. Read every set bonus before slotting; one missed **two-piece** can halve your effective damage.
25.lore:
The **eclipse** came at midday and never left. Within a single rotation, the kingdom's spires bled fire, the cathedral choirs fell silent, and the Vault — sealed since the first age — cracked at its seam.
      The **fallen knights** are the ones who answered the bell. They marched into the breach in gleaming order and emerged as something else. Now they patrol the ruins in slow, ceremonial loops, blades dragging across stone.
      You are the last vanguard to remember the **sealing rites**. Your gear is older than the kingdom that minted it. Each loadout you assemble is half preparation, half remembrance — a wager that the old combinations still hold against what the Vault has become.

faq.q: How does the auto-battle actually resolve?
faq.a: Once you confirm a loadout, your vanguard fights waves automatically using the gear, runes, and potions you slotted. Damage, defense, and ability triggers are derived from the grid layout — adjacency between matching pieces produces synergy effects that scale your output far beyond raw item stats.

faq.q: What is grid adjacency and why does it matter?
faq.a: Every gear piece you place on the grid checks its four neighboring cells for matching tags. A flame-blade beside an ember rune adds burn-over-time; a shield beside a vitality flask trades attack speed for survival. Two identical loadouts arranged differently can produce wildly different damage and survival numbers.

faq.q: What are legendary anchor pieces?
faq.a: Anchor pieces are top-tier gear that reshape entire builds. They are rare drops from late chapters and bosses, and they usually demand a specific cluster of supporting gear to function. Save anchors for builds you've already validated in early chapters rather than forcing a run around an unfamiliar piece.

faq.q: Why did my run end so fast?
faq.a: Most early losses come from isolated runes — a rune placed without a matching weapon neighbor contributes almost nothing. Re-check adjacency before confirming, make sure at least one set bonus is active, and dedicate a column to potions if you're losing to drawn-out boss phases.

faq.q: Does the game support mobile?
faq.a: Vault of Ashes: Fallen Era is PC only. The tactical grid requires precise click and drag input for loadout assembly and gear rotation, which the current build does not adapt to touch screens.

26.title: Neon Stack
26.description: A one-tap neon stacking arcade — drop sliding slabs onto a rising tower, slice off every overhang, and chain perfect drops to regrow your width as the slab gets faster.
26.fullDescription:
Neon Stack is a **one-tap timing game** set over a synthwave skyline. A glowing slab slides back and forth above your tower — tap to drop it. Whatever hangs past the block below is **sliced off and falls as debris**, and the trimmed piece becomes your next, narrower target. Miss the tower completely, or leave a sliver under 8 px wide, and the run is over.
      Land within **7 px** of dead-center (10 px on touch) and it counts as a **perfect drop**: the slab snaps flush, nothing is cut, and the tower **regrows 6 px** of width — up to its starting size. Consecutive perfects build a **combo counter**; any imperfect drop resets it. Your score is simply **blocks stacked**, and your **best combo streak** is saved alongside it as a secondary stat.
      The slab speeds up with every level — **230 px/s** at the base, +9 px/s per block, capped at **620 px/s** — and alternates its entry side each row, so the rhythm you find early won't hold forever. Pseudo-3D neon blocks, depth fog down the tower, shard bursts on every cut and a self-playing demo behind the menu keep the skyline alive.
      Simple to start, brutal to master. How high can you build before one mistimed tap topples the run?
26.controls: Click / Tap / Space / Enter / Down Arrow: drop the sliding slab onto the stack. Time the release so it lands flush over the block below — a perfect drop keeps everything, regrows width and extends your combo. Language and mute toggles sit in the top corners.
26.tips: Watch the **slab's edge**, not its center — edges are where the overhang gets sheared. Perfect drops **regrow 6 px** of width, so a run of clean chains can rescue a narrowed tower; protect what you have, because one greedy drop leaves a sliver that nothing regrows in time. The slab **accelerates every level** and swaps its entry side each row — re-find the beat after every few blocks instead of tapping on the old rhythm. On phones the perfect window is wider (10 px), so trust your finger a little more than your eyes.
26.lore:
Above the synthwave city, the **old broadcast tower** fell dark decades ago. The signal that built it never stopped transmitting — block by block, frequency by frequency, it still tries to climb back toward the channel it lost.
      Every player who taps in lends the signal a hand. Each clean align is a frequency locked, each combo a verse of the song that once lit the whole skyline. Miss the rhythm and the tower narrows, the neon dims, and the signal starts again.
      No one has reached the top. Your best is just how close the signal got before the rhythm broke.

faq.a: Every block you place adds one — that is the score. Your best combo streak (the longest run of consecutive perfect drops) is tracked separately and reported as a secondary stat; it does not multiply the score.

faq.a: Releasing the slab within 7 px of dead-center over the block below (10 px on touch). It snaps flush, nothing is sliced, the tower regrows 6 px of width (up to its starting size) and your combo counter goes up. Any wider offset slices the overhang off as debris and resets the combo.

27.title: Kingdom of Ashes - Fallen Era
27.description: A deep single-player roguelike deck-builder — draft a deck run by run, chain elemental resonances, and push a branching map of battles, shrines and bosses through a kingdom burned to ash.
27.fullDescription:
Kingdom of Ashes - Fallen Era is a **turn-based roguelike deck-builder** set in Alea, a kingdom the **Dicefall** left in cinders. You do not bring a deck to a run — you build one inside it. Every run opens on a small signature core plus a draft you make yourself, so the same hero plays differently every time depending on what the draft offers and what you are brave enough to skip.
      Combat is turn-based and mana-driven. Cards carry elements — fire, ice, lightning, shadow, blood, nature, holy and more — and playing them in the right order triggers **Resonance**, the game's core combo layer. Stack the elements a card wants and a single turn snowballs; stack them wrong and you spend a turn setting up a hit that never lands. **Block, burn, bleed, freeze and curse** all interact, and the enemy telegraphs its intent so every decision is yours to read.
      Between fights you choose a path through a **branching map**: elite gauntlets, shops, rests, shrines, merge nodes, army waves and treasure caches. Each branch trades safety for power. Beyond the run itself sits the meta layer — **ash currency**, a forge shop, hero mastery levels, **ascension tiers** that raise the difficulty ceiling and a bestiary that fills in as you meet what lives out there. Losing a run is how you get stronger for the next one.
      The web edition ships two heroes: the **Knight**, the balanced all-elements opener, and the **Inquisitor**, a punishing bleed-and-holy build that rewards aggression. Both play the full campaign — same map, same relics, same bosses, same ascension ladder. The complete **41-hero roster** and the DLC packs live in the Steam release.
      The kingdom is already ash. What you build on the way down is the only thing that survives it.

Spend gold on removing a bad card before you spend it on adding a good one. **Losing is progression**: ash, mastery levels and forge upgrades all carry into the next run, so a dead run still moved you forward.
27.lore:
**Alea** was a kingdom that **settled its arguments by roll**. Every law, every succession, every border was decided by the dice, and for a long age that was enough. Then came the **Dicefall** — the throw that came up wrong, and kept coming up wrong, until the spires burned and the ash covered the fields.
      What survived did not survive whole. Knights kept their oaths to a crown that no longer sits anywhere. Inquisitors kept their fire and lost the thing it was meant to purify. The elements themselves came loose from the order that once held them, and now they answer to whoever can put them in the right sequence.
      You descend into the fallen era carrying nothing but what you can draft on the way down. The kingdom will not be saved. But something is still down there deciding the rolls, and it can be reached.

faq.q: What is Resonance?
faq.a: The combo layer. Cards carry elements, and playing them in the sequence a card is looking for triggers a bonus effect on top of its printed one. It is why a focused two-element deck usually beats a pile of individually stronger cards — the payoff is in the ordering, not the raw numbers.

faq.q: Is losing a run a total loss?

28.title: Barrack Defense
28.description: A wave-based defense game where you build barracks instead of towers — seven unit types train and fight on their own while you hold the Center Command against endless waves of ground and air attackers.
28.fullDescription:
Barrack Defense is a defense game with **no towers** in it. What you place are **barracks**, and what fights for you are the units they train — **soldiers, archers, knights, rogues, brutes, bombardiers and falconers** that walk out on their own, pick their own targets and hold the ground you gave them. Your job is deciding what gets built, where it stands, and what it costs you.
      Every barrack is also a building with **hit points**, so placement is a wall as much as a factory. Push production out toward a lane and it soaks the first hit; tuck it behind the keep and it survives but arrives late. **Rams and gargoyles** come specifically for your barracks, hitting them for double, so a defense that never loses a building is a defense that was probably built too far back.
      Combat runs on real numbers: **armor mitigates physical damage, pierce halves it, magic ignores it entirely**. A rogue's fast four-damage flurry bounces off a tank's plate while a brute's single twenty-damage swing goes straight through. Bleed, slow and burn stack on top. Every enemy that arrives is a question about which of your seven types answers it, and the answer changes as the roster grows.
      Waves come in two phases — an **eight-second build countdown** with no enemies on the field, then the assault itself, arriving down one lane early and splitting across more roads as the run deepens. Bosses land **every fifth wave**, mega-bosses every tenth, and from wave ten on they bring their own air escort. There is no final wave. The run ends when the **Center Command** falls, and the only question is how far you got.

28.tips: Buy your first upgrade before your fourth barrack — a **Lv.2 type** out-produces a second building of the same type for less gold. Keep one Falconer or Archer up before **wave 6**; imps fly straight past a wall of ground-only melee and the keep has no answer of its own. Armor is the whole puzzle: send brutes and bombardiers at tanks and rams, rogues at swarms, and never expect a rogue to chew through plate. **Right-click repairs** cost a fraction of a rebuild, so patch a damaged barrack during the build phase instead of watching it die on the next push. When gold outpaces your buildable ring, plant a **Frontier** and start a second front rather than stacking everything on the keep.
28.lore:
The **Center Command** was never meant to be a fortress. It was a **muster hall** — the place where the kingdom's levies were counted, fed and sent north. The walls it has now were added in a hurry, by people who already knew the north had stopped sending anything back.
      What comes down the roads now does not negotiate and does not besiege in any way the old manuals describe. **Rams** walk past armed defenders to break the training halls instead, and the things with wings do not use the roads at all. Whoever is directing them understands that an army you cannot replace is an army already beaten.
      So the muster hall musters. Barracks go up in the mud around it, turn out whoever they can train in the minutes they are given, and those recruits walk out to meet the road. Some of them come back. The hall keeps counting.

faq.q: How is this different from a normal tower defense?
faq.a: Your buildings never attack. A barrack trains a unit on its own timer, and that unit walks out, finds the nearest enemy it can hit and fights there until it dies or the enemy does. You control what gets produced and where it is produced from — not who shoots what. It also means your production line is on the battlefield: barracks have hit points and can be destroyed.

faq.q: Which barrack type should I build first?
faq.a: Soldiers at 40 gold are the cheapest way to get bodies on the field, and bodies are what keep enemies away from the keep early. Add an Archer or Falconer before wave 6 — that is when flying imps arrive, and ground-only types cannot touch them. From there, build toward what the wave preview shows: brutes and bombardiers for armored pushes, rogues for swarms.

faq.q: What does armor actually do?
faq.a: Armor mitigates incoming physical damage as a fraction, so it blunts many small hits far harder than a few big ones. Pierce damage halves the target’s armor and magic damage ignores it completely. That is why a rogue’s 4-damage flurry bounces off a 24-armor tank while a brute’s 20-damage swing lands nearly in full, and why bombardiers are the reliable answer to a clustered, armored wave.

faq.q: Can I repair a barrack that is nearly destroyed?
faq.a: Yes — right-click a damaged barrack to repair it back to full for a share of its cost, scaled to how much health is missing. Right-clicking a barrack at full health sells it instead for a 50% refund, which is the cheap way to reshape a lane between waves.

faq.q: Is there a final wave?
faq.a: No. The waves keep coming and keep scaling, with a boss every fifth wave and a mega-boss every tenth, plus extra attack lanes opening as the run gets deeper. The run ends when the Center Command reaches zero health, and your best wave and best score are saved in your browser between sessions.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone?
faq.a: It loads and the layout stacks, but it is built for a mouse and a wide screen — placement precision, right-click repair and the barrack panel all assume a desktop. Play it on a PC for the intended experience.

29.title: Shadow Runner
29.description: A fast, unforgiving katana action-roguelike. Chain three-phase combos into aerial dives, take curses for stacked rewards, and cut down through a collapsing corridor. This is the free Chapter 1 demo of the Steam release.
29.fullDescription:
Shadow Runner is a **side-scrolling action-roguelike** about one runner, one katana and a descent that does not let you back out. Every chapter is a short stack of waves fought on a hand-built map: enemies arrive in scripted groups, the field has to be cleared before the next one spawns, and clearing a wave hands you a choice of **upgrade cards** that reshape the rest of the run.
      Combat is built for expression rather than button-mashing. The light attack runs a **three-phase combo** that flows into an air slash; the heavy button is a super, an aerial dive and a ground plunge depending on where you are when you press it; **dash and dive-cancel** let you rewrite your spacing mid-fight. Hit-pause and a short slow-motion beat land on every clean kill, so a combo that reads well also feels like it landed. A **sub-weapon slot** — drone, grenade, knife, disc, tether or skull — sits on top of all of it and gets swapped to fit the run you are actually having.
      Between chapters you come back to the hub: a shop that rolls a fresh card selection, an equipment NPC, a mannequin for your inventory, a codex, a fountain, and the **Echo shrine** where run currency turns into permanent meta upgrades. Before a chapter starts you can take a **Pact of Curses** — opt into penalties in exchange for stacked rewards, reshaping the rules of that specific run. Loot drops carry affixes, set bonuses and run-defining uniques.
      This web build is the demo: **Chapter 1, The Corridor**, plus the tutorial, the hub, the shop, the challenge arena and the full meta layer. Gold, gear and **Echo upgrades** persist between runs in your browser, so the roguelike loop is intact — the descent just stops at the first landing. The Steam release continues from there with **11 more chapters**, two side campaigns, endless mode and the rest of the bestiary.

Keyboard or gamepad — the game is built around a controller and remaps every button in Settings.
29.tips: **Do not mash Z**. The **three-phase combo** has a rhythm, and the **third hit** is where the damage is — a dropped combo costs more than a slow one. Dash is an escape and a repositioning tool, not a movement key; save a charge for the moment a wave closes on both sides. **X in the air** is a dive that carries through a target, so use it to break out of a crowd rather than to open on one. **Take curses early**: the reward stacking compounds over a whole run, and Chapter 1 is where the penalty costs you least. Spend at the **Echo shrine** before you spend at the shop — meta upgrades survive the run, shop cards do not.
29.lore:
**The signal breaks**. There are no commands left on the channel, only the hum of something much older underneath it, and the runner is already too far down to be recalled.
      The **corridor** was built to move things one way. Whatever was being moved stopped arriving a long time ago, and what walks it now was not on the manifest. The blade answers before the runner does.
      There is no retreat written into the descent. There is only the **next landing**, and the thing waiting on it.

Chapters 2 to 12, the Volcano and Underworld side campaigns, endless mode and the later bosses are in the Steam release.

faq.q: Does my progress carry over to the full game?
faq.a: No. The demo saves to your browser's local storage and the Steam build keeps its own save, on Steam Cloud. What carries over is what you learned about the combo timing.

faq.q: Is there a leaderboard?
faq.a: Not on the web. Score and best wave are stored locally in your browser, and the Steam release pushes them to a Steam leaderboard instead. Nothing is uploaded from this page.

faq.q: Can I play with a controller?
faq.a: Yes. The game was built for a gamepad and every button is remappable in Settings. Keyboard works just as well — the default layout is arrows to move, Space to jump, Z and X to attack, C to dash.

faq.q: It is too hard. Is there an easier setting?

30.title: AshenKeys
30.description: A keyboard-driven incremental where every key you hit is a strike and typing a skill’s keyword casts it — you have no health and cannot die, but every foe regenerates, so the only way down the ladder is out-damaging the wall in front of you.
30.fullDescription:
AshenKeys is a clicker played on the **whole keyboard**. Any printable key is a basic strike, and the three cast slots under the fight each show a keyword from your **six-skill deck** — type "fire" and Fireball lands, type "frost" and Frostlance freezes the foe’s regeneration. A cast spends its slot, which redraws a random skill from the deck and goes on cooldown, so what you can cast next is never quite what you just cast.
      There is **no health bar** on your side. You cannot die, and nothing here attacks you. What every enemy does instead is **regenerate** — a share of its max HP every second, more for elites and bosses, and more again past Level 20 — and that is the whole difficulty curve: if your **damage per second** sits under the stage’s regeneration, the bar refills faster than you empty it and the fight is flagged as stalled. No stage fields a lone foe, either: two guards flank the common, elite or boss in the middle and take every hit until they fall.
      Landing hits close together builds a **combo**, and combo is the engine. It lifts crit and double-strike chance on every hit and keeps climbing past 100%, where strikes land three and four at a time, and it multiplies skill hits on top. Let it lapse for a second and a half and it falls back to zero. Three trees feed the same hot path: Attack Mastery from basic hits, a Skill Mastery tree per skill levelled by its own casts, and a Passive Tree grown from points that foes drop. From Level 11 you can ascend, trading the run for Ash that buys permanent ranks.
      Gold goes to the **War Camp**. After every boss the Spoils screen opens the Forge — Blade, Focus, Censer and Sigil, gear for basics, skills, regen shred and crits — and the Camp, where five mercenaries can be hired and two fly a banner beside you, striking again, echoing casts or stretching your combo window. Mid-fight, the Satchel sells oilstone, iceflask, warpaint and elixir, and you use one by typing its name.
      **Twenty-four skills across eight elements** bring burn, freeze, poison, curse, bleed, a shock that arcs, a smite and a neutral strike, with longer keywords unlocking as you beat the Level 20, 40 and 60 bosses. A hundred hand-painted foes from ten courts fill the **Monster Codex**, each with a line of lore; every elite and boss carries a name, and **every tenth level** is a boss you engage by typing that name. The ladder does not end. Your progress saves in your browser.

30.tips: Fill all six deck slots before you push — skills only cast from a full deck, so until then the cast slots read "Not Enough Skills" and every key is a basic; open Skill Mastery and **right-click** skills to equip them. Keep hitting: combo resets after about a second and a half without a basic, and the crit and double-strike chance it grants is worth more than any single upgrade early. When a bar refills instead of dropping, that is the **regeneration wall** — spend points or gold rather than grinding the stalled foe. **Freeze** cuts regeneration per stack, the Forge’s **Censer** shreds it for the rest of the run, and an **iceflask** stops it outright for six seconds. Put each skill’s eight points into two main upgrades rather than spreading them over three. Once a run stalls past Level 11, **ascend**: Ash pays five per level reached, and your deck, skill unlocks and Codex carry over.
30.lore:
The keep taught its scribes that language is a tool for pinning things down. Write a name correctly and the thing it names holds still long enough to be measured, filed and forgotten. That was the theory, and for a long stretch of quiet centuries it was also true.
      What lives below the keep now learned the same lesson from the other side. **Names hold it still**. So the descent is made by **typing**: a word struck cleanly is a blade, and a word struck the wrong way is nothing at all — a keystroke spent on air while the thing in front of you knits itself back together.
      Nothing down there can hurt the one holding the keys, which the scribes found reassuring until they understood what it meant. You are not in danger. You are simply not strong enough yet, and the dark can wait longer than you can.

faq.q: Why is nothing happening when I type a keyword?
faq.a: Your deck is not full yet. Skills only cast once all six deck slots hold a skill; until then the cast slots read "Not Enough Skills" and every key falls through to a basic strike. Open Skill Mastery from the left rail and right-click skills to equip them. Six-, seven- and eight-letter keywords also stay locked until you beat the Level 20, 40 and 60 bosses.

faq.q: The enemy health bar keeps refilling. What am I doing wrong?
faq.a: Nothing — that is the game’s only fail state. Every foe regenerates a share of its max HP each second, and if your damage per second is below the stage’s total the bar wins and a STALLED warning appears next to your 20-second DPS readout. Spend points, freeze or shred the regeneration, throw an iceflask, or come back after a few more upgrades.

faq.q: Can I die?
faq.a: No. You have no health, enemies never attack you, and there is no defeat screen. The pressure is entirely economic: a foe you cannot out-damage costs you time, not a run.

faq.q: What does combo actually do?
faq.a: Hits landed close together stack a combo that raises crit chance and double-strike chance on every hit — about 80% at 150 combo and 99% at 500 — and keeps climbing past 100%, where hits land three and four at a time and crits hit harder. Combo also adds skill power, up to +200%. Stop basic-striking for about a second and a half and it resets; boss fights open with a short grace period.

faq.q: How does skill progression work?
faq.a: Every skill levels from its own casts. Each level adds skill power and, up to Level 8, one point for that skill’s tree: a free core plus three main upgrades drawn from effects such as Splash, Chain, Echo, Detonate and Execute, each with ranks II–IV. Eight points max out two of the three, so every skill is a choice. Basic hits level a separate Attack Mastery tree, foes drop points for the Passive Tree, and ascending turns a run into Ash for the Ascension tree.

faq.q: What is the War Camp?
faq.a: Where your gold goes. On the Spoils screen after each boss you buy Forge levels (Blade, Focus, Censer, Sigil) and hire Camp mercenaries, two of whom act at once. Mid-fight, the anvil on the left rail sells Satchel items, which you use by typing their name. Everything gold buys resets when you ascend.

faq.q: What do I keep when I ascend?
faq.a: Ascension unlocks at Level 11 and pays Ash, five per level reached (more with Ash Harvest). You keep your deck, Ash, Ascension ranks, skill unlocks, lifetime stats and the Monster Codex; your level, gold, War Camp and the Attack, Skill and Passive trees start over.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone?
faq.a: Not really. Everything is typed — basics, casts, item names and boss names — so it is built for a physical keyboard. On touch devices such as Steam Deck or a touch laptop a ⌨ button raises the on-screen keyboard, but on a phone the screen is too cramped. Play it on a PC.

31.title: Debt & Dragons
31.description: An idle tower where five floors each print gold a different way — crack dragon eggs, scrape sigil scrolls, drop plinko pearls, bank dice hands, brew potions — all to pay off a Warden whose toll goes up every single time you clear it.
31.fullDescription:
Debt & Dragons is an idle game about a debt that is designed never to be paid. You live in a wizard's tower you do not own, the **Warden** at the door holds the ledger with your name in it, and the only way out is the toll. Clear it and the Warden simply reads you a bigger number — it set the first one after looking at your purse, and it will set the next one the same way.
      Each of the five floors is its own small game with its own feel. The **Roost** is a throwing game: drag back from the rock pile, land hits on a dragon egg until it cracks, and every wyrmling that hatches is a permanent +5% to gold on every floor. The **Scrivener's Nook** is a scratch card — buy a sealed scroll, scrape the wax off, match three sigils, and watch the Crown take its 20% tithe on its own line until you hire someone to make that line go away. **Mana Falls** is plinko with a gilded gate hidden in the middle bin and gutters down both sides. The **Oracle's Table** is five bone dice, hold what you like and pay to chase the rest. The **Cauldron** is a brewing bench where recipes are discovered, never given.
      Only one number in the game is multiplicative, and it is the **dice multiplier** — which bleeds 2% a minute back toward 1, so the Oracle is a fire you keep feeding rather than an income stream you park. Everything else stacks flat: hatchlings, the permanent +25% behind the Mana Falls jackpot gate, Golden Sigils that tick gold per second forever. **Eighteen potions** make no gold at all; they rewrite the other floors' rules instead, and only two can be active at once, so brewing is a build choice. **Fifteen familiars** hide behind conditions nobody tells you about — idle for five minutes and something wanders in to keep you company — and once hired they automate the floors you are tired of clicking.
      Close the tab and the tower keeps working: offline progress runs the same logic ticks the live game does, capped at eight hours and credited at half. When the toll finally breaks you, walk out through the Warden's Gate, mint Scales, and spend them on six permanent branches that make the next run start further along. Or go the other way — find three of the right reagent, brew the **Draught of Erasure**, and pour it over the ledger until your name is not in the book at all.

31.tips: Throw at the fractures, not the shell — a body hit chips 1, a hit on a glowing fracture chips 10. The Crown's **20% tithe** on scroll payouts is not a display bug; the **Goblin Accountant** is the fix, so hunt it early. In **Mana Falls** the outer two lanes are gutters that pay nothing, and the narrow gate inside the centre bin is a permanent **+25%** to everything — aim middle even when the side bins look safer. The **dice multiplier** decays **2% every minute** toward 1, so bank a hand before you go do something else, or brew the **Hourglass Brew** to halve the bleed. Potions are a build, not income: two slots, eighteen recipes, and nothing stops you dropping three reagents in to see what happens. Before you close the tab, note that offline income is capped at 8 hours — the **Wisp** raises that to 14 — and pays at 50%, so a quick check-in beats a long one.
31.lore:
The tower was a loan. Nobody remembers taking it out, which the **Warden** considers a poor argument and a common one. What is written in the **ledger** is your name, a number, and the standing terms: the tower is yours to use and the number is the Warden's to set.
      So you work the floors. You throw rocks at eggs because hatchlings pay, you scrape wax off scrolls because the Crown lets you keep four fifths, you feed pearls to a waterfall that mostly eats them. And when you finally stack the coins on the ledger, the Warden takes the pile without counting it — it already knows the number, it has always known the number, and the number has already gone up.
      Somewhere in the cauldron room there is a **third way**. Three measures of the right nothing, brewed correctly, and the ink lifts off the page like it was never dry.

32.title: Endless Runner
32.description: A three-lane sprint through deep space where an obstacle's colour is its answer: red means tap, amber means hold, violet means switch lanes, green means keep your feet down. Ten obstacle types, twenty-one runners to wear, and a speed that only ever climbs.
32.fullDescription:
Endless Runner is a **three-lane runner** built entirely out of primitives — every texture in it is drawn on a canvas the moment the game loads, so there is not a single sprite sheet in the download. You run down a track suspended in space, under nebulae and spiral galaxies, toward a wormhole that never gets any closer. **Metres are the score**. There is nothing else to collect but coins, and nothing to do with coins but buy your way back into the run.
      The whole game is one rule: **colour is the answer**. A **red hurdle** is a tap-jump. An **amber tall block** needs the button held — the longer you hold, the higher you go. A **violet block** cannot be jumped at all, so change lanes. A **green hopper** bounces over your head, so stay on the ground and let it pass. Five more obstacles bend those answers instead of adding new ones: a deep-red stomper lands exactly where you are standing, a rose window has a hole a tap fits through and a hold does not, a green archway punishes any jump at all, a violet slider sweeps across the lanes and parks in one of them, a red scuttler hunts your lane until the last ten metres, and a gold thief is the only thing on the track that is not lethal — it just takes your coins.
      Speed climbs from the first step and never stops, but rows are spaced by time rather than distance, so the window you get to read an obstacle narrows on purpose rather than collapsing. **Every 200 metres** the run crosses into a new region — Indigo Reach, Ember Belt, Cryo Drift, Verdant Spine — and the palette, the finish on every surface and the whole sky ease over into the new one mid-stride. The hue family never changes, because the hue is the answer.
      Coins go into a single wallet that pays for everything: a shield mid-run, a revive when you die (the price doubles every time you use it in the same run), a coin magnet, a shield on every start, and **twenty-one runners** — Three Kingdoms generals, a boba cup, a bowl of ramen, five planets, and one ink dragon. Wearing a runner earns it chest pins by mileage, **eleven tiers** from Basic to Void, and the last of them is fifty thousand metres in one skin. Everything saves in your browser, and the game speaks English, Korean and Japanese.
32.controls: Space / ↑ / W: Tap to hop, hold to jump higher / A · D or ← →: Switch lanes / S: Buy a shield mid-run / Enter: Start or retry / Touch: Tap to jump (how long you hold is how high you go), swipe left or right to change lane, swipe up for a full-height jump
32.tips: **Read the colour, not the shape** — red is a tap, amber is a hold, violet means move, green means keep your feet on the track. The **rose window** is the one trap that punishes a good habit: a tap fits through the hole, a held jump hits the lid. The **green archway** punishes every jump, so run straight at it. When the **violet slider** is sweeping across the lanes, the lane it has already left is the safe one — it parks ten metres before it reaches you. The **red scuttler** tracks your lane, so switching early does nothing; tap over it instead. The **gold thief** costs coins, never the run, so never throw a run away dodging one. Buy the shield before the speed makes you want it, and remember a **revive doubles in price** every time you take one in the same run.
32.lore:
The track was laid by nobody anyone remembers, through **four regions** that keep coming back around: a clean neon reach, a sun-baked belt, a frozen drift lit from inside, and a spine of things that glow on their own. **Every two hundred metres** the light changes hands and the whole sky follows it over.
      The **wormhole** at the end of the track has never got any closer, which nobody who runs here considers a problem. The distance behind you is the only number the track keeps, and it keeps it under whichever face you happened to be wearing.

faq.q: How do I know what to do with an obstacle?
faq.a: By its colour. Red is a tap-jump, amber needs the jump held, violet cannot be jumped so change lanes, green wants you on the ground, and gold is a thief that takes coins instead of your run. Zones change the shade and the finish of everything, but never the hue family — so the answer you learned in the first region is still the answer in the fourth.

faq.q: The window has a hole in it. Why did my jump still hit it?
faq.a: Because you held it. The window's gap fits a bare tap and nothing more — a held jump carries you straight into the lid above it. It is the one obstacle where jumping higher is the wrong idea, and its twin is the green archway, where jumping at all is.

faq.q: Does the game get unfair at high speed?
faq.a: Rows are spaced by time, not by distance, so the seconds you get to react shrink on a tuned curve rather than disappearing. The generator also re-rolls any row that would leave you no reachable lane, and it never puts a three-door gate — the row nobody can jump — directly after a row that needed a full-height jump.

faq.q: What are coins for?
faq.a: One wallet pays for everything. Mid-run: a 100-gold shield that absorbs one hit, and a revive that starts at 40 and doubles with each use in the same run. Between runs: a coin magnet, a shield on every start, and runners at 60 gold each.

faq.q: Do the 21 runners change how the game plays?
faq.a: No — they are cosmetic, and that is deliberate. What they do carry is their own mileage: the pin on a runner's chest steps up through eleven tiers as you run in it, starting at 500 metres and ending at 50,000. Switching runners starts that climb over, so a wardrobe is fifteen separate commitments rather than one.

faq.q: Does my progress save, and can I play on a phone?
faq.a: Progress, gold, owned runners and per-skin mileage all save in this browser. Touch is fully supported — tap to jump with hold length driving the height, swipe sideways for lanes, swipe up for a full jump — and the game runs in English, Korean and Japanese.

33.title: Flux Tower Defense
33.description: A grid tower defense where the maze is yours to draw: towers block the path, traps sit on it, and every run hands you a random arsenal to build around. Elemental attributes at Lv 5, Tier 2 abilities at Lv 10, natural disasters you click away, ten elite modifiers on the way. This is the free web edition of the Steam release — waves 1 to 10.
33.fullDescription:
Flux Tower Defense is a **grid-based tower defense** on a 19×15 board with no fixed lane. Enemies pour out of a red portal and walk the shortest route to your teal fortress, recomputed the instant anything changes — so **towers are walls** and where you put them is the map. Wall Towers are cheap and only there to bend the path; every other tower shoots. Traps are the opposite: they sit on the route and fire when something walks over them. Sell a tower and the path snaps to the new opening before the next enemy takes a step.
      You do not pick your build from a menu. Every run **drafts a loadout at random** from 40 towers, auras and specials plus 15 traps, and you plan around what you drew; every five waves you draft one reward on top. Each tower levels from 1 to 15: Lv 4 and 9 are per-tower enhancements, **Lv 5 rolls an attribute** — LAVA, GLACIER, ELECTRIC or STEEL — that changes how the tower behaves and looks, **Lv 10 upgrades it to Tier 2** (burn, freeze, chain, crit), and Lv 15 rolls a second one. Four towers can attempt an **Evolution** at max level: a 60% roll that either transforms them or knocks them back to Lv 4. Towers also earn kills toward veterancy ranks, and Tier 3 unlocks a permanent perk pick.
      The waves push back. Every wave from the second carries a boss; regular enemies can spawn with one of **ten elite modifiers** — Haste, Shielded, Armored, Juggernaut, Regen, Phasing, EMP, Frenzied, Vampiric, Phoenix; some species carry permanent passives like Fireproof or Burrow. Between waves a **natural disaster** can hit — meteor, blizzard, earthquake, tornado, thunderstorm — and you click its hotspot down before the timer runs out or it takes a tower with it. Tollgates let you mortgage a stretch of the path for gold at the cost of a speed buff to whoever crosses. Three difficulties change enemy HP, gold, starting life and the wall cap; a Daily Challenge hands everyone the same map and loadout for one attempt.
      This is the **web edition**: waves 1 to 10, saved in your browser, in 11 languages. The run ends with the fortress standing when wave 10 is cleared. The Steam release is the full game — endless waves, a second portal that opens at wave 10 and more after it, the Challenger boss, the **New Discovery** content (VOID and BLIGHT elements, the reroll-only SUPERIOR, Prisma rerolls and five Power-Up star tiers past max level), Steam achievements, leaderboards and cloud saves.

33.tips: **Build the maze first, the damage second** — a long snaking path past a few towers beats a short path past many. **Wall Towers are the cheapest cell on the board**; use them to bend the route, not to fight. Read your **loadout** before placing anything: a run with Frost Plate and Tesla Coil wants a different corridor than one with Blade Launcher and Tar Pit. Push one carry tower to **Lv 5 early** for its attribute roll rather than spreading gold across six Lv 3s. When a **disaster** lands, click its hotspot — the towers under it are the price of ignoring it. **Sell to reroute** when a boss gets past your kill zone; the path updates instantly. A **second portal opens at wave 10** — leave yourself gold for it.
33.lore:
The flux is what the old maps called the seam where the portal side and the fortress side meet — a stretch of ground that never stays the same shape twice. Build on it and it holds. Leave it empty and something walks across.
      Nobody who holds a fortress on the flux draws their own arsenal. It arrives, it is what it is, and the ones who last are the ones who learned to shape the ground to the tools instead of wishing for other tools. Ten waves is the proving run. What comes after is the war.

faq.a: Waves 1 to 10 on every difficulty, the full random loadout draft, the Lv 1–15 upgrade path with attributes and Tier 2 abilities, evolutions, veterancy, elite modifiers, natural disasters, tollgates and the Daily Challenge. The run ends with a clear screen once wave 10 is finished. Endless waves, the extra portals, the Challenger boss and the New Discovery content are in the Steam release.

faq.q: Why did my enemies suddenly take a different route?
faq.a: Because you changed the board. The path is the shortest walkable route from the portal to the fortress and it is recomputed every time a tower is placed or sold. Towers block; traps and tollgates do not. If a placement would seal the fortress off completely, the game refuses it and warns you.

faq.q: Does my progress save?
faq.a: Yes — the run auto-saves at every wave clear and on pause, in your browser's local storage, and the main menu offers Continue. Clearing site data or playing in a private window wipes it, and it does not carry over to the Steam build, which keeps its own save on Steam Cloud.

faq.q: Is there a leaderboard?
faq.a: Not on the web. Your best waves-cleared count is stored locally on this site. The Steam release submits to all-time, weekly and daily Steam leaderboards and unlocks 20 achievements.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone?
faq.a: No. The board needs right-click to sell, drag to lay walls and a hover-driven detail panel, and the 19×15 grid is laid out for a desktop screen. Play it on a computer.

Personal Travel Diary is a **travel planner and tracker** on a 3D map you fill yourself — not a game. Start a diary with a name and a start and end date and it lays out one day per date. Type a place into the search box — suggestions appear from the first letter, biased to wherever the map is looking — and it becomes a stop on the chosen day, with the leg from your previous stop drawn in. 35.title: Color Spin Rush
35.description: A one-touch reflex arcade game: colored marbles drop toward a spinning disk and you hold the screen to turn it, catching each marble in the slot of its own color. Combos multiply every catch, new colors join as your score climbs, three misses end the run. 55 skins to collect, each a full theme.
35.fullDescription:
Color Spin Rush is a **one-touch reflex arcade game**. A ring with five colored slots sits near the bottom of the screen and marbles fall toward it from above. **Hold to spin** — the longer you hold, the faster the disk turns; let go and it glides to a stop. Line up the slot that matches the falling marble's color before it lands and it drops through for points. Catch it in the wrong color, or let it miss, and you lose one of **three lives**.
      Every catch in a row raises your **combo**, and each catch pays **10 × combo** points, so a long streak is worth far more than careful singles. The run starts with two colors; a new one joins every 150 points until all five are in play, and marbles already in the air are cleared without penalty when the disk reshuffles. Levels climb with your score, marbles arrive more often, and fall speed rises until level 8 — fall time scales to your screen, so a small phone and a tall tablet get the same reaction window.
      Every 500 points earns a **coin**, and a daily bonus adds five more. Coins unlock **55 skins**, and each one is a whole theme rather than a recolor: its own marble art (pixel, gem, candy, planet, lava, circuit and more), disk design, animated backdrop and button style. The game over screen counts up your final score and shows your best combo, level reached and coins earned. Music and effects are written in C Dorian with separate volume sliders; plays in English, Korean and Japanese, installs as an app and works offline.

35.tips: **Tap in short bursts** — the disk keeps gliding after you let go, so a quick tap moves it one slot while a long hold overshoots. **Watch the lowest marble**, not the newest one; it lands first. **Protect the combo**: each catch pays 10 × combo, so a 20-catch streak is worth more than a hundred careful singles. When a **new color joins**, the marbles in the air are cleared for free — use the pause to re-read the slot order. Claim the **daily bonus** for five coins toward the next skin. The **ink** skin gives every color its own pattern, which helps if some colors are hard to tell apart.
35.lore:
The ring does not care what you meant to do. It only knows where it stopped. Every marble is a question with one right answer, and you have about a second to find it with a thumb.
      Two colors is a warm-up. Five colors is a conversation. Somewhere past a thirty-catch combo the spinning stops feeling like reaction and starts feeling like rhythm.

38.title: Only NAND
38.description: A logic-circuit puzzle game where you start with a single part, the NAND gate, and build everything else from it. Wire NOT, AND, OR and XOR, then adders, multiplexers, latches, counters and a tiny ALU. Every circuit you solve becomes a chip for the next one, across 43 levels and a free-build sandbox.
38.fullDescription:
Only NAND is a **logic-circuit puzzle game** built on one real idea from computer engineering: every digital circuit can be made from **NAND gates alone**. You start with one part and two switches. Drag wires from pin to pin, flip the inputs, and press Test circuit — the game checks your design against every row of the truth table and marks the ones that don't match.
      Each solved level **becomes a chip** in your parts list. Build NOT out of NAND, then AND out of NOT and NAND, then OR, XOR, a half adder, a full adder and a **4-bit adder** — each one standing on the last. Tap the magnifier on any chip to **look inside** and see the NAND gates it comes down to, using your own design.
      **43 levels in six chapters**: Basics, New Gates, Advanced (adders, subtractors, multiplexers), Expert (decoder, comparator, multiplier, a 2-bit ALU, a 7-segment display), **Memory** — feedback loops, latches, flip-flops, counters and a shift register, tested step by step over time — and **Special Rules**, classic puzzles with NAND only and a hard part budget. Finish under **par** for three stars. Every level has a hint, a short "why it works" note and a Wikipedia link.
      The **Sandbox** is a huge free-build board with every part unlocked: place switches and lamps, box-select and move groups, draw named regions, watch a live truth table, save circuits and share a PNG of your design. Circuit-board look with light and dark mode, D Dorian ambient music and effects with volume sliders. Plays in English, Korean and Japanese, installs as an app and works offline.

38.tips: Every gate starts from **NOT**: tie both NAND inputs together and it inverts. **AND is NOT of NAND**, and **OR is NAND of two NOTs** (De Morgan). Use the chips you already built — an adder is much easier from HALF and FULL than from bare NANDs. Stuck? In **Memory** levels a wire that loops back is the point, not a mistake.
38.lore:
Every processor ever made, from a pocket calculator to the chip in your phone, comes down to billions of tiny switches. Wire four transistors the right way and you get a NAND gate — and with enough NAND gates, you can build anything.

42.title: One Minute: Auto-Battle
42.description: Survive the swarm as a tiny slime that shoots on its own. Pick one of three tiered upgrade cards every 10 seconds, then at each minute decide: keep fighting for more PARTS or bank what you have.
42.fullDescription:
One Minute: Auto-Battle is a **top-down auto-shooter survival roguelite**. You are a tiny glowing slime in an endless dark arena, and you only steer: the slime fires at the nearest monster in range on its own. Eye-orb drones pour in from every side, elite and boss mechs hover in on cyan jets, and every 20 seconds the waves grow bigger and nastier.
      Power comes from the clock, not from grinding. **Every 10 seconds** the game pauses and offers **three upgrade cards** from a pool of 33 in four categories — attack, defense, utility and special. Each card rolls a **tier from 1 to 10**; tiers 5 and 10 add milestone effects, and Luck (+2 on every level-up) pushes the odds toward the rare high tiers. Explosive Rounds, Chain Lightning, Vampirism, Barrier, Orbiting Blades, Phoenix Feather — one strong pick can turn a run.
      Every minute is a checkpoint. Keep going for another 60 seconds, or **take what you have earned** and bank your **PARTS**: monsters drop them now and then and bosses always do, but die before you cash out and they are gone. PARTS buy nodes in the **GAME UPGRADE** tree — 46 nodes in six branches (Hunt, Forge, Arsenal, Vault, Clock and Pact). Unlock special cards, rerolls, banish and lock, insurance and interest, **Overtime** to stretch a run to five minutes and finally Endless; switch on **Pacts** such as Glass Slime or Rush Hour to make runs harder for a bigger payout.
      The arena fights back too. **Elemental pillars** project Ice, Fire, Electric and Mud fields that slow, burn, power up or trip both you and the monsters, and overlapping fields of the same type multiply. Hand-shaded pixel art, D Dorian music and effects with a volume control, pause with live tier odds, a mid-run save that resumes with a 3-2-1 countdown, and English, Korean and Japanese text round it out. Plays on phone, tablet and desktop, installs as an app and works offline.

42.tips: **Keep moving in wide circles** — standing still lets the swarm close the ring around you. Early on, take **attack speed and damage** so you can clear the waves; once Luck climbs, high-tier cards are worth more than a new card at tier 1. Pull monsters into **Ice and Electric fields**, and stay out of **Fire** yourself unless you have HP to spare. Bank your PARTS at the checkpoint whenever a run feels shaky — dying throws them all away. Spend your first PARTS on **Overtime I** in the Clock branch: longer runs pay more.
42.lore:
Down in the dark under the old arena, a drop of glowing slime woke up with one minute to live. Then the drones opened their eyes.
      It cannot run forever and it cannot hide. All it can do is shoot, grow stronger every ten seconds, and carry what it salvages out before the clock — and the mechs — catch up.

faq.q: Do I have to aim or shoot?
faq.a: No. The slime fires at the nearest monster in range by itself. You only move — dodging the swarm and steering monsters into the right pillar fields is the whole skill.

faq.q: What are PARTS and how do I keep them?
faq.a: PARTS are the upgrade currency. Normal monsters drop one rarely, elites more often, and every boss drops one. They are only safe once you choose Take What's Earned at a minute checkpoint; if you die first you lose them, unless you have bought Salvage or Checkpoint Insurance in the Vault branch.

faq.q: Why does my run end at one minute?
faq.a: The first run cap is one minute. Buy Overtime I–IV in the Clock branch to extend it to five minutes (each tier needs a run that reached the current cap), then Endless removes the limit.

faq.q: What counts as my personal best on ArcadeDeck?
faq.a: Your longest survival time in seconds. A run that ends at a checkpoint counts the same as one that ends in death.

faq.q: Can I play on a phone?
faq.a: Yes. Drag anywhere to use the floating joystick and tap cards to pick them. It installs as an app and plays offline, and a run in progress is saved if you close the page.

43.title: Marble Racing
43.description: A 3D party decision-maker for 2–20 players. Each animal rides a glass marble down a glowing toy marble run, and the finishing order decides winners, ranks, teams, penalties or who pays the bill.
43.fullDescription:
Marble Racing is the 3D sequel to Ladder Game: a **party decision-maker** for **2 to 20 players**. Every player is a cute animal riding inside a clear glass marble, and the results wait at the finish, one for each place. Send everyone down a glowing toy marble run and the finishing order decides who gets what.
      Type your own result for each place or use **Quick fill**: Winner (the first places), Penalty (the last places), Rank, Teams (sizes even to within one), Ratio (random percentage shares) or Bill — a random split of a total in dollars, won or yen that always adds up exactly, with as many people paying nothing as you choose.
      Press Start and a fresh course is built from a new seed. A **flyover** shows it off, pausing on each mod's neon sign, everyone is seated at a random start gate, and Race! counts down 3-2-1-GO. The camera follows the action, the standings update live, and you can tap any animal to follow its marble or press **×3** to fast-forward. A close finish on a place that decides something gets a **photo finish** in slow motion.
      Pick **Short, Medium or Long** (about 25, 30 or 50 seconds) and fill its 3, 5 or 7 slots with **mods**: carousels, wormholes, trap routes, a mist tube that hides who is ahead, boomerang half-pipes, waterslide bowls, ramps, jumps with boost hoops, boost pads, a narrow helix of glass coils, mud, a whirlpool, the Wormhole Roulette, a fork switch and trapdoors — or let Random mods pick new ones every race. Peg boards scatter the pack on every course, and a hard knock from behind stuns the marble in front.
      Most races hide a **Joker** on one place: whoever finishes there trades results with a fairly drawn player at the very end. A summary with places, finish times and split checkpoints, a record of your last 30 races, the code of every course, D Dorian music and effects with a volume control, and English, Korean and Japanese round it out. With **Phone link** one phone hosts and up to 15 others watch the same race live on their own screens. Plays on phones, tablets and desktop; installs as an app and works offline.

A marble run on the kitchen table has always been the fairest referee: nobody can push a marble, and nobody can argue with gravity.
      Here twenty animals squeeze into glass marbles at the top of a neon toy track under the night sky. Somewhere below, a wormhole is humming, the carousel is turning, and one finishing cup might hide the Joker.

44.title: Emotion Act
44.description: A party acting card game for 2–27 players on one phone. Say an everyday line with a secret emotion and see who can tell Wronged from Betrayed.
44.fullDescription:
Emotion Act is a **party acting card game** for **2 to 27 players** that needs nothing but one phone. Three piles sit on the table: a Number card from 1 to 6, an Emotion card listing six numbered feelings, and a Line card with an everyday sentence like "This is really good."
      Each round a reel picks the actor. Everyone else looks away while the actor sees the secret number and the emotion card, then the line appears: **5 seconds to think**, then **15 seconds to act** it out loud with that feeling while the others watch the screen. Everyone guesses the number from 1 to 6, and once per round the group can ask for **+10 sec more acting**.
      The emotion cards are the trick: each one hides two or three near-twins (Wronged · Betrayed · Hurt, Nervous · Anxious · Urgent), so a good guess reads nuance, not just the mood. **Scoring** pushes the actor to be clear but not obvious: if nobody gets it the actor loses 2, if everyone gets it the actor loses 1 and everyone gains 1, and if only some get it the right guessers gain 2 while the wrong ones lose 1.
      Everybody acts once in shuffled order, then **3 bonus rounds** with random actors and no penalties shake up the standings before the **curtain call**, with a spotlight, confetti and the Star of the night. Two players get their own rule (right +1, wrong −1), and one player gets endless acting practice.
      The lobby's Cards choice swaps the middle pile. **Situation** cards (10 cards, 60 situations) list six reasons for one feeling without ever naming it: the actor says the line as the person in that situation and everyone guesses which situation it was, played sitting with hands on knees, face and voice only. Mix draws one of the two piles each round.
      With **Phone link** one phone hosts and the others join with a 4-letter code: each phone picks its player, the actor reads the secret cards on their own phone and everyone enters their own guess. 10 emotion cards with 48 emotions, 30 line cards in each language, a colour for every player, D Dorian sound effects with a volume control and English, Korean and Japanese round it out. Plays on phones, tablets and desktop, installs as an app, works offline and saves after every step.

44.tips: Pick a number whose emotion has a twin on the same card? Lean into what makes it different. Acting too obviously costs you a point when everyone gets it, and nobody getting it costs two. Not sure? Ask for **+10 sec more acting** before anyone picks. Playing in a big group? Use **Phone link** so the actor can peek at their own phone and nobody has to look away.
44.lore:
Every drama club warms up the same way: one plain sentence, said ten different ways, until the room can hear the difference between sad and heartbroken.
      Here the curtain is a phone screen, the script is three cards, and the audience gets to judge. Somewhere between Wronged and Betrayed is the Star of the night.

45.title: Animal Racing
45.description: A couch kart racer for 1–4 players in split screen or on linked phones. Twenty chibi animals in wind-up toy karts drift, boost and throw bombs across four neon tracks, and the finishing order can settle a prize, a penalty or the bill.
45.fullDescription:
Animal Racing is a **couch kart racer** for **1 to 4 players** and the racing sister of Ladder Game. Everyone picks one of **20 chibi animals**, each in its own glossy wind-up toy kart — Rabbit's Carrot Rocket, Penguin's Ice Sled, Panda's Bamboo Buggy, Hamster's Wheel Runner — and CPUs fill the rest of the field (4, 6 or 8 racers). Two to four players **split the screen**, joining with any mix of keyboard, gamepads and touch. Or use **Phone link**: one phone hosts with a four-letter code, up to three others join, and every phone races its own kart on its own full screen.
      Driving is arcade, not sim. Hold Drift through a corner to charge cyan, amber and pink sparks into a **mini-turbo**, hit the gas right before GO for a **rocket start**, run over glowing rung strips for a boost and collect star coins for extra top speed. Glass "?" cards roll one of four items: a Bomb to throw ahead or drop behind, a Bubble shield, a Lucky Dash and the Joker, which swaps places with the racer just ahead. Wormholes fling you forward — or back — and spinning turntables push the pack sideways.
      Four tracks: the Toy Diorama Speedway in a child's room at night, the watercolour Storybook Meadow with its plank bridge over the river, the Neon Arcade Circuit floating in space and Festival Night under Korean lotus lanterns and fireworks. Race one in Quick Race or all four in a **Grand Prix** for points, in Chill, Normal or Turbo. Turn on **Party Stakes** and the finishing order decides a Winner, a Penalty, a Rank, two Teams or who pays the most of the Bill.

Every night, when the lights go out, the toy box opens. Twenty animals wind up their karts, the night-light becomes a stadium lamp and the blanket turns into a mountain pass.
